Montalegre
mohn-tah-LEH-greh
n. (the Catalan charterhouse of 1415 near Barcelona, still a living community)
Catalan mont alegre, the cheerful or glad mountain.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Santa Maria de Montalegre at Tiana, north of Barcelona, was founded in 1415 by the union of two earlier Carthusian houses, Sant Pol de Mar and Vallparadís. It was sacked in the Napoleonic wars, suppressed in 1835, and reoccupied; it survived the burning of churches in the Spanish Civil War, when the monks were dispersed and some killed, and the community is there still, keeping the full Carthusian observance. This dictionary records Montalegre for its name, the glad mountain, because gladness in Scripture is commanded rather than merely permitted, and it is not the same thing as circumstances being pleasant. Joy is named as strength, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). Its location is given, “in thy presence is fulness of joy” (Psa 16:11). It is a thing God himself effects by exchange, “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11), and it is twice commanded by an apostle writing from prison, “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines joy as a delight of the mind from the consideration of good; gladness as joy or pleasure of the mind; to rejoice as to experience joy; mirth as merriment; and cheerfulness as a state of moderate joy.

expand to see more

JOY, n. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; that excitement of pleasurable feelings which is caused by success or good fortune.

GLADNESS, n. Joy, or a moderate degree of joy and exhilaration; pleasure of mind; cheerfulness.

REJOICE, v.i. To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations.

MIRTH, n. Social merriment; hilarity; noisy gayety; jollity; noisy laughter.

CHEERFULNESS, n. Life; animation; good spirits; a state of moderate joy or gayety; alacrity.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:10 — "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

Psa 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Psa 30:11 — "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;"

Phi 4:4 — "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice."

Modern Corruption

Catalan charterhouse of 1415, the glad mountain: sacked, suppressed, dispersed in the Civil War, and keeping the full observance still.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture makes joy a strength rather than a mood. Nehemiah says it to people who had just wept at hearing the law read, and he tells them to stop and eat, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). The psalm locates it in a presence rather than in a set of conditions, “in thy presence is fulness of joy” (Psa 16:11).

The second thing is that the exchange is God's to make. David does not describe cheering himself up; he describes a reversal done to him, “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11). And the command to rejoice comes from a man under guard, repeated so that no reader can treat it as a remark about the weather, “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4). A house called the glad mountain that has been sacked three times has as much right to the name as anyone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chedvah (H2304), gladness; Hebrew simchah (H8057), joy; Hebrew machol (H4234), a dance; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice; Hebrew ma'oz (H4581), strength.

expand to see more

Hebrew chedvah (H2304) — gladness, named as strength; “for the joy of the LORD is your strength”, Nehemiah 8:10.

Hebrew simchah (H8057) — joy, full in his presence; “in thy presence is fulness of joy”, Psalm 16:11.

Hebrew machol (H4234) — a dance, exchanged for mourning; “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing”, Psalm 30:11.

Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, to overturn; “Thou hast turned for me my mourning”, Psalm 30:11.

Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, commanded twice; “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice”, Philippians 4:4.

Usage

"“for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10) — said to people who had just wept."

"“Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11) — a reversal done to him."

"“Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4) — written under guard, and repeated."
